title: CircIKBKB promotes hepatocellular carcinoma stemness and EMT via TAF15-PTCH1-mediated Hedgehog activation.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) represents one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Accumulating studies in recent years have confirmed that circular RNAs (circRNAs) are involved in the regulation of tumor initiation and progression. Nevertheless, the precise functions and underlying molecular mechanisms of circRNAs in HCC remain to be thoroughly investigated. In this study, we identified a circular RNA derived from the IKBKB gene, designated circIKBKB (database accession number: hsa_circ_0084102), which exhibits significantly elevated expression in HCC cell lines. Functional experiments demonstrated that circIKBKB promotes HCC cell proliferation, sustains cancer stemness properties, and induces epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Mechanistically, circIKBKB directly interacts with the RNA-binding protein TATA-box binding protein associated factor 15 (TAF15) and suppresses its polyubiquitination-mediated proteasomal degradation, thereby maintaining intracellular TAF15 protein stability. The upregulated TAF15 further binds to Patched 1 (PTCH1) mRNA and enhances its transcript stability, which consequently drives aberrant activation of the Hedgehog signaling pathway. Both in vitro and in vivo validation assays confirmed that overexpression of PTCH1 partially reversed the phenotypic effects induced by circIKBKB knockdown. Collectively, our findings uncover the regulatory mechanism of circIKBKB in mediating aberrant activation of the Hedgehog pathway in HCC, and this work may provide a potential interventional strategy for HCC treatment.

title: FXR2 Promotes Autophagic Clearance of Sindbis Virus Capsid and Protects Against Viral Encephalitis.
abstract: Autophagy protects neurons from viral infection by removing toxic viral components, but the host factors that recognize viral proteins and direct their clearance remain incompletely defined. Here, we identify fragile X mental retardation syndrome-related protein 2 (FXR2) as a mediator of protective autophagy during Sindbis virus (SINV) infection. Quantitative proteomic analysis of host proteins associated with SINV capsid identified FXR2, an RNA-binding protein linked to stress granules and protein homeostasis. Co-immunoprecipitation and immunofluorescence confirmed that FXR2 associates and colocalizes with viral capsid in infected cells. Loss of FXR2 increased capsid accumulation, reduced LC3 lipidation and autophagosome formation, and impaired p62 degradation following infection. Reconstitution of FXR2-deficient cells restored autophagy and promoted capsid clearance. Although FXR2 deficiency did not significantly increase viral replication, it enhanced virus-induced cell death, suggesting that FXR2 protects infected cells by limiting viral protein toxicity rather than by directly restricting virus production. Consistent with this model, both Fxr2-null and heterozygous mice exhibited increased mortality following neurotropic SINV challenge, and Fxr2-null mice developed greater neuronal degeneration, inflammation, and cell death despite viral titers comparable to those in wild-type animals. Together, these findings identify FXR2 as a previously unrecognized component of the antiviral autophagy pathway that promotes viral capsid clearance and protects neural tissue from infection-associated damage.

title: PmiREN3.0: a multi-omics integrated and AI-assisted encyclopedia for plant microRNA research.
abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are key post-transcriptional regulators in gene regulatory networks (GRNs). Comprehensive research on miRNAs increasingly requires the integration of large and heterogeneous datasets, together with more efficient approaches to knowledge exploration. Here, we present PmiREN3.0, a major update of the Plant MicroRNA Encyclopedia. Compared with PmiREN2.0, species/subspecies coverage increased from 179 to 340, adding 22 orders, 51 families, and 108 genera. Using the same standardized workflow and annotation criteria as previous releases, high-confidence miRNAs were identified from 5319 small RNA sequencing (sRNA-seq) datasets, with miRNA loci increasing from 39 751 to 87 667 and miRNA families from 7838 to 18 389. Resources and tools from previous releases were extensively updated, while six new modules were added for primary transcripts, DNA methylation, RNA modifications, stress-responsive expression, metabolic pathways, and core GRNs. PmiREN3.0 also introduces miRai+, a knowledge service powered by artificial intelligence (AI) that combines a language model fine-tuned on miRNA knowledge with retrieval augmented generation. Evaluation yielded scores of 0.910 for answer relevance, 0.965 for faithfulness, and 0.906 for factual correctness. Together, PmiREN3.0 provides an expanded plant miRNA dataset and an integrated platform combining multi-omics data and AI-assisted knowledge services for plant miRNA research. PmiREN3.0 is available at https://pmiren.com/.

title: Cytoplasmic TDP-43 aggregation promotes oxidative stress and neurotoxicity through Trx1 mRNA sequestration and translational suppression.
abstract: Transactive response (TAR) DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) is a multifunctional DNA/RNA binding protein. Cytoplasmic TDP-43 aggregation is a pathological hallmark of diverse neurodegenerative diseases collectively termed TDP-43 proteinopathy. Oxidative stress is closely associated with TDP-43 aggregation and neurotoxicity in TDP-43 proteinopathy, yet the underlying molecular mechanisms remain elusive. To delineate molecular basis of TDP-43 proteinopathy, we conducted deep quantitative proteomic profiling using a Neuro-2a (N2a) neuronal cell model of human wild-type TDP-43 overexpression (N2a-hTDP-43). We identified thioredoxin-1 (Trx1) as a central node linking mitochondrial dysfunction and redox dysregulation to TDP-43 pathology. Consistent with this, TDP-43 overexpression markedly reduced Trx1 protein levels. Moreover, inhibiting Trx1 exacerbates, whereas overexpressing Trx1 alleviates, cytoplasmic TDP-43 aggregation and neurotoxicity in N2a-hTDP-43 cells. Furthermore, overexpressing Trx1 alleviates TDP-43-associated pathologies in mouse primary neurons. Notably, we identified that cytoplasmic TDP-43 protein sequesters Trx1 mRNAs into insoluble TDP-43 inclusions, leading to its translational suppression. We also demonstrated that suppression of Trx1 is a core mechanism eliciting oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in TDP-43 overexpression model. Importantly, in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived motor neurons (MN) harboring the pathogenic TDP-43 M337V mutation (TDP-43M337V iPSC-MNs), Trx1 expression is downregulated, concomitant with increased oxidative stress, compared to the isogenic TDP-43WT iPSC-MN control. Furthermore, inducing Trx1 expression markedly reduces oxidative stress and cytoplasmic TDP-43 aggregation in TDP-43M337V iPSC-MNs, suggesting conserved neuroprotective role of Trx1 in TDP-43 proteinopathy in human. Collectively, we identified Trx1 as a pivotal regulator of TDP-43 proteinopathy, highlighting therapeutic potential of Trx1 for TDP-43 proteinopathies.

title: BPR-30901649, An Angiotensinogen-Targeting Small Interfering RNA, Achieves Ultra-Durable Target Silencing and Sustained Blood Pressure Reduction Through 20 Weeks in Hypertensive Non-Human Primates.
abstract: Hypertension affects over 1.3 billion adults worldwide, and poor adherence to daily oral therapy contributes to inadequate blood pressure (BP) control. We characterized BPR-30901649, a liver-targeted small interfering RNA (siRNA) against angiotensinogen (AGT), hypothesizing that its optimized design would confer greater potency and durability than an advanced clinical-stage AGT siRNA benchmark. BPR-30901649 was selected through in vitro and in vivo screening in HepG2 cells and human AGT (hAGT) transgenic mice. Off-target risk was assessed by RNA sequencing in primary human hepatocytes. Pharmacodynamics were evaluated in hAGT mice after single and repeat subcutaneous (SC) dosing, and in hypertensive cynomolgus monkeys given a single SC dose of 1.5 or 3.0 mg/kg, with serum AGT and systolic BP (SBP) monitored for 20 weeks. Investigational New Drug (IND)-enabling toxicology was conducted in rats and nonhuman primates (NHPs). RNA sequencing indicated low off-target risk. In hAGT mice, BPR-30901649 produced significantly deeper serum AGT knockdown than the benchmark. In hypertensive NHPs, a single SC injection produced rapid, dose-dependent, and sustained AGT suppression; at week 20, SBP remained reduced by 14.2% (20.3 mm Hg) and 17.3% (25.3 mm Hg) in the low- and high-dose groups, respectively. In repeat-dose toxicology, the no-observed-adverse-effect level was 100 mg/kg in NHPs. BPR-30901649 surpassed an advanced clinical-stage AGT siRNA benchmark in vivo and showed a wide preclinical safety margin, supporting its clinical development as a potential twice-yearly therapy for hypertension.

title: Structural insights into West Nile virus programmed ribosomal frameshifting reveal coordinated regulation by RNA, ribosome, and nascent peptide.
abstract: Programmed -1 ribosomal frameshifting (-1 PRF) is essential for West Nile virus (WNV) gene expression and generates NS1', a protein implicated in viral replication and pathogenesis. However, the structural pathway by which translating ribosomes traverse the WNV frameshift signal remains poorly understood. Here, we combined cryo-electron microscopy, RNA structural modeling, molecular dynamics simulations, and functional analyses to investigate the mechanism of WNV -1 PRF. We resolved a pre-frameshift ribosomal complex together with four translocation intermediates, including a previously uncharacterized semi-rotated state in which the 40S subunit undergoes partial rotation while tRNAs remain in near-canonical A/A-P/P configurations. This intermediate is accompanied by remodeling of conserved peptidyl-transferase-center nucleotides, suggesting that active-site rearrangements can precede canonical tRNA movement during translocation. Structural modeling and simulations further suggest that the WNV frameshift-stimulatory RNA exists as a compact but conformationally heterogeneous ensemble capable of adopting multiple stable or metastable pseudoknot architectures. In addition, we identified direct interactions between the nascent viral peptide and the ribosomal exit tunnel, and disruption of the tunnel-occupying peptide reduced frameshifting efficiency. Together, our findings suggest that WNV frameshifting is governed not by a single stimulatory element but by the coordinated coupling of RNA dynamics, ribosome remodeling, and nascent-chain interactions.IMPORTANCEViruses often rely on a process called programmed ribosomal frameshifting to produce proteins important for infection. West Nile virus (WNV), a mosquito-borne pathogen that can cause severe neurological disease in humans, uses this strategy to generate NS1', a protein linked to viral replication and pathogenesis. However, how ribosomes are redirected into an alternative reading frame remains incompletely understood. Here, we provide structural insights into ribosome movement during translation of the WNV frameshift signal. Our findings also suggest that the viral RNA can adopt alternative conformations and that the emerging viral peptide may influence frameshifting efficiency. Together, these observations contribute to our understanding of how RNA structure, ribosomal dynamics, and nascent peptides may influence viral protein expression.

title: DoriC 14.0: an updated database of prokaryotic replication origins with significantly expanded plasmid oriV annotations.
abstract: Replication origins are essential for both chromosome duplication and plasmid maintenance; however, their annotation remains challenging across different replicon types and across diverse phylogenetic lineages. DoriC 14.0, the latest update of the database of replication origins in prokaryotic genomes, restructures and greatly expands this resource, with particular emphasis on plasmid replication. The latest release contains 530 178 computationally derived origin records, associated with 432 232 distinct sequence accessions, including 434 060 chromosomal and 96 118 plasmid records from bacteria and archaea. For bacterial plasmids, OriV-Finder was applied with RNA II-based refinement, whereas a customized OriV-Finder pipeline was employed for archaeal plasmids, which relies on archaeal replication-associated proteins and origin recognition box motifs. DoriC 14.0 combines literature evidence with computational predictions, maintains traceable record identifiers, and offers versioned data with release history. New features include comparative sequence support, related-origin links, interactive candidate replication initiation protein (RIP) sequence-similarity networks, plasmid-level analyses of origin recurrence, RIP profiles, and RNA II variation. The updated website provides filter-based browsing, record-level views, BLAST searches, and standardized downloads, and is freely accessible at https://tubic.org/doric/ and https://tubic.tju.edu.cn/doric/ without registration.

title: Genome-Wide Characterization of HERV-Derived RNA Regulatory Potential in the Human Transcriptome.
abstract: Human endogenous retroviruses (HERVs) comprise nearly 8% of the human genome, and their long terminal repeats (LTRs) are well-established sources of transcriptional regulatory elements. However, their contribution to RNA-level regulatory features remains largely unexplored. Here, we present a genome-wide characterization of the RNA regulatory potential of 53,176 HERV internal regions and 560,594 LTRs. We found 16.2% more predicted RNA-binding protein motif occurrences in HERV internal regions than expected after controlling for dinucleotide composition. At the subfamily level, overall motif abundance was elevated in HERVH but remained close to expectation in HERVK (HML-2). Conserved retroviral protein domains incorporated into transcripts were mostly located in exceptionally long terminal exons, approximately 7-fold longer than those of other multi-exon transcripts. HERV internal sequence overlapped 4,074 annotated long noncoding RNA genes and accounted for more than 80% of the gene body of 144, most of them functionally unannotated. Finally, 6,583 unique antisense LTRs at transcript termini formed SPARCS-like candidate configurations that could support antisense RNA pairing; protein-coding genes carrying them in 3' untranslated regions showed enrichment for immune signaling and recombination-related terms. These results provide a genome-wide framework of candidate HERV-derived RNA regulatory features and transcript architectures for experimental testing.

title: Plasma-membrane proteins in human skeletal muscle for targeted drug delivery: An annotated resource.
abstract: Skeletal muscle is essential for metabolic regulation, energy homeostasis, and physical function. Its dysfunction contributes to disorders such as type 2 diabetes, muscular dystrophies, sarcopenia, cachexia, and muscle wasting linked to aging, cancer, and immobilization. Despite advances in RNA-based therapeutics, achieving efficient and selective delivery to skeletal muscle remains a major translational barrier. Targeting muscle-enriched cell-surface proteins represents a promising strategy to improve therapeutic specificity while limiting systemic exposure. Here, we combine a systematic literature review with database-driven analyses to identify and prioritize skeletal muscle-enriched plasma membrane proteins as candidate entry points for targeted delivery. The review summarizes current targeting approaches, highlighting their strengths and limitations. In parallel, integrative mining of the Human Protein Atlas, Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx), and CellxGene datasets identified 76 high-confidence skeletal muscle-enriched membrane-associated proteins. These were further functionally annotated and ranked using multi-parameter criteria, including relevance to internalization and suitability for nucleic acid-based delivery. In addition, we discuss potential disease contexts in which to employ these. Together, these analyses generate a curated resource of candidate targets and provide a conceptual framework for developing next-generation delivery platforms for RNA therapeutics and other modalities aimed at skeletal muscle across a broad range of muscle-related diseases.

title: Rotavirus NSP1 activates human NLRP1 inflammasome.
abstract: While inflammasomes detect and defend against pathogens, the precise mechanisms by which enteric viruses trigger these complexes, and the specific viral components involved remain incompletely understood. In this study, we demonstrate that rotavirus infection robustly induced human NLRP1 inflammasome activation via p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK)-dependent and -independent pathways. Utilizing cell lines reconstituted with NLRP1 signaling and reverse genetics-rescued recombinant rotaviruses, we identified non-structural protein 1 (NSP1), a well-characterized viral antagonist of host interferon signaling, as an activator of the NLRP1 inflammasome in the absence of double-stranded RNA. Domain mapping analysis revealed that the C-terminus of NSP1 but not the C-terminal IRF3-binding site was essential for triggering inflammasome activation. Mechanistically, we show that NSP1 induced the proteasomal degradation of NLRP1 to elicit its activation, a process dependent on host neddylation pathways and the Cullin-3/Elongin B/C ubiquitin ligase complex. Together, these findings suggest that RV engages parallel NLRP1 surveillance pathways, including a p38-dependent response to infection, and a novel NSP1-dependent pathway involving the ubiquitin-proteosome system, where a viral strategy aimed at host protein degradation inadvertently trips the human NLRP1 inflammasome wire. When rotavirus infects the gut, it uses a viral protein called NSP1 to shut down key immune defenses of host cells. However, human cells have an immune sensor called NLRP1 that acts as a tripwire. When NSP1 attempts to force the destruction of NLRP1, the disposal process itself accidentally triggers the NLRP1 alarm. This causes an explosive inflammatory cell death that alerts the immune system. This discovery reveals how a viral strategy to suppress host immunity backfires, offering new insights into viral gut inflammation and future vaccine design.

title: ProtoPure: Literature Mining and Analysis of Protein Purification Protocols at Proteome Scale.
abstract: Protein purification is a fundamental step for analyzing individual proteins and protein complexes and identifying interactions with other proteins, DNA, or RNA. A variety of protein purification strategies exist to address desired scale, throughput, and downstream applications. However, selecting an effective experimental procedure remains a largely empirical process that a quick literature review can help guide. Researchers typically survey on the order of a dozen publications for proteins with similar biochemical properties, assessing conditions on a case-by-case basis, leaving no systematic framework for comparison and decision-making at the scale of entire protein families. As protein engineering and design evolve, identifying effective purification conditions remains critical for obtaining sufficient quantities of properly folded and functional proteins. To address this gap, we developed ProtoPure, an LLM-based workflow and database that automates the extraction, standardization and analysis of protein purification conditions from peer-reviewed literature at scale. Given a user-defined UniProt table-enabling flexible selection of proteins by family, organism, or proteome. ProtoPure retrieves associated publications, classifies them based on the presence of purification protocols, and extracts a standardized set of 12 purification parameters (e.g., buffer composition, elution conditions). By transforming dispersed experimental descriptions into a structured resource, ProtoPure makes it possible to compare purification strategies across thousands of proteins. The resulting dataset revealed quantitative convergence toward a limited set of recombinant expression practices, with BL21(DE3)-based systems dominating protein production and recurrent combinations of expression host, inducer, growth medium, and plasmid occurring substantially more frequently than expected by chance. In contrast, downstream purification parameters exhibited greater diversity, revealing a workflow architecture that combines standardized expression infrastructure with more flexible biochemical components.

title: Diversity and evolution of the ribovirian class Stelpaviricetes.
abstract: Metatranscriptome mining has dramatically expanded the known diversity of ribovirians at all taxonomic levels. We explored the class Stelpaviricetes in the phylum Pisuviricota that currently includes three orders and six recognized virus families: order Stellavirales with family Astroviridae infecting vertebrates; Patatavirales with families Potyviridae, the largest known family of plant ribovirians, and Potyliviridae; and Hypofuvirales consisting of three families of viruses associated largely with phytopathogenic fungi. Using an order-specific collection of Hidden Markov Model profiles for the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP), the hallmark protein of ribovirians, we identified 103 putative families within Stelpaviricetes, most of which share an astrovirus-like genome architecture, encoding three protein domains: the RdRP, a chymotrypsin-like protease, and a single jellyroll capsid protein. The topology of the phylogenetic tree of the RdRP implies that the common ancestor of Stelpaviricetes had an astrovirus-like genome. The ancestor of the order Patatavirales acquired two additional domains, a papain-like protease and a superfamily 2 helicase, whereas the capsid protein was replaced with an unrelated one, forming filamentous capsids. The ancestor of Hypofuvirales also encoded a superfamily 2 helicase and a papain-like protease, but had lost the capsid protein. Hypofuvirales might have derived from Patatavirales or evolved independently from an astro-like ancestor. For the vast majority of Stelpaviricetes identified in metatranscriptomes, host assignment remains elusive. Nevertheless, analysis of endogenous virus elements and isolated viruses provides some clues suggesting that the common ancestor of Potyviridae and Potyliviridae had a fungal host, whereas the common ancestor of Stelpaviricetes might have been a protist virus.IMPORTANCEThe enormous diversity of viruses on Earth is only now coming to light through extensive metagenome and metatranscriptome mining. Using vast databases of ribovirus genomes, we performed phylogenomic analysis of the class Stelpaviricetes, which includes the families Astroviridae and Potyviridae, the former comprising animal viruses and the latter comprising plant viruses. We identified more than 100 family-level groups of viruses, most of which have small, astrovirus-like genomes, likely resembling the common ancestor of Stelpaviricetes. In contrast, the putative common ancestor of Potyviridae and its sister family Potyliviridae exhibits higher genome complexity that apparently emerged in viruses of fungi. The most plausible scenario for the origin of Potyviridae involves horizontal transfer of a virus across kingdoms between plant-associated fungi and plants.

title: Structural basis of ribosomal RNA repair by RtcB2
abstract: Ribotoxins disable ribosomes by cleaving ribosomal RNA, but how repair enzymes recognize and restore these damaged machines remains unclear. Here, we report three cryo-electron microscopy structures of the RNA ligase RtcB2 bound to damaged Escherichia coli 30S subunits. An extended interface stabilizes the ribosomal head and decoding-center scaffold while positioning the cleaved 3'-phosphate end within the catalytic pocket. Two structures contain enzyme-linked guanosine monophosphate, whereas the third captures its transfer to the RNA. RNA activation accompanies RtcB2 reorientation and entry of the 5'-hydroxyl-containing segment into an adjacent cleft. Comparisons with assembled ribosomes reveal structural barriers to substrate access. These structures connect recognition of a damaged ribosome to chemical activation of its RNA for repair.

title: Plant potassium channel β-subunits confer antiviral defense via disrupting potyviral 6K2-mediated vesicle maturation and trafficking.
abstract: Potyviruses constitute the largest known group of plant RNA viruses. Their 6K2 protein is an integral membrane protein that induces the formation of vesicular structures, which support viral RNA replication and act as vehicles for intracellular movement. While multiple host proteins are known to regulate either viral replication or movement, it remains largely unclear whether and how a single host protein can coordinately modulate both processes. Here, we identify NbKNB1, a Nicotiana benthamiana homolog of the plant potassium channel β-subunit. Genetic assays demonstrate that NbKNB1 confers antiviral activity against turnip mosaic virus (TuMV). NbKNB1 localizes predominantly to the plasma membrane in healthy cells, but relocalizes to 6K2-induced viral replication complexes during TuMV infection. Biochemical analyses show that NbKNB1 directly interacts with 6K2, disrupting 6K2 self-association and impairing the maturation of 6K2-tagged vesicles. NbKNB1 also competes with the viral cylindrical inclusion (CI) protein for 6K2 binding, thereby inhibiting TuMV cell-to-cell movement. A 6K2-binding-deficient mutant, NbKNB1Δ270-279, fails to restrict both viral replication and intercellular movement, confirming that direct interaction with 6K2 is required for NbKNB1-mediated suppression of TuMV infection. Moreover, NbKNB1 and its maize homolog ZmKZB1 also reduce infection by other potyviruses. Collectively, these findings reveal a novel antiviral strategy in which plant potassium channel β-subunit homologs target the viral 6K2 protein to counteract potyvirus infection, and provide a promising target for antiviral breeding.

title: Suramin inspires next-generation broad-spectrum antiviral design targeting RdRps.
abstract: Structural studies of diverse viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerases reveal that the broad-spectrum antiviral Suramin binds distinct sites while repeatedly exploiting conserved RNA-interacting and electrostatic features. This Pearl highlights common vulnerabilities within viral RNA polymerases and discusses how structural studies provide a framework for future antiviral design.

title: Dihydrotanshinone I in Paired Vemurafenib-Sensitive and Resistant A375 Melanoma Cells.
abstract: Acquired resistance limits the response to vemurafenib in melanoma. This study investigated dihydrotanshinone I (DHT) in parental A375 cells and a vemurafenib-resistant derivative (A375R). An exploratory computational workflow combined target prediction, survival associations, tumor-versus-normal expression comparisons, dependency screening, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) Cox regression, and random survival forests. Heat shock protein 90 alpha family class A member 1 (HSP90AA1) and signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) were prioritized for cellular testing. Cellular thermal shift assays showed DHT-associated thermal stabilization, and combined small interfering RNA depletion produced greater phenotypic effects than single-target depletion. Eight drug combinations yielded Chou-Talalay combination indices of 0.520-0.940 in A375R cells. Transcriptional changes and lipid-peroxidation readouts were consistent with altered resistance-associated and oxidative-stress programs. Together, these findings support further investigation of HSP90AA1 and STAT3 in the response of resistant melanoma cells to DHT.

title: METTL3-associated YTHDF1-COX-1 axis is linked to reduced antiplatelet response to aspirin in older adults.
abstract: This study explores the role and mechanism of RNA m6A methylation in reduced antiplatelet response to aspirin in older adults. A total of 34 patients aged ≥60 years routinely receiving 100 mg/d aspirin were enrolled. Based on light transmission aggregometry (LTA), subjects were divided into a low-response group (n = 14, platelet aggregation rate (PAR) ≥12 %) and a high-response group (n = 20, PAR ≤7 %). Patients with a low aspirin response exhibited higher levels of m6A, accompanied by elevated methyltransferase-like 3 (METTL3) and YTH N6-methyladenosine RNA binding protein 1 (YTHDF1) (p < 0.05). Serum levels of prostaglandin H2 (PGH2) and thromboxane B2 (TXB2) were also elevated in the low-response group. Spearman correlation revealed that PAR and PGH2 were positively correlated with both METTL3 and YTHDF1 mRNA, while TXB2 positively correlated with METTL3 mRNA (p < 0.05), indicating the association of m6A degree with aspirin response. Mechanistically, METTL3 overexpression in MEG-01 cells enhanced megakaryocyte proliferation and upregulated YTHDF1, which subsequently increased the translation efficiency of cyclooxygenase 1 (COX-1) mRNA and elevated COX-1 protein. RNA immunoprecipitation confirmed that YTHDF1 directly bound to COX-1 mRNA in a METTL3-dependent manner. The METTL3/YTHDF1-COX-1 axis may attenuate the antiplatelet efficiency of aspirin by modulating AA metabolism and megakaryocyte function, providing a potential biomarker and target for aspirin low-responsiveness.

title: Augmenting the Cytotoxicity of Anticancer Peptide K6L9 by In Vitro-Synthesized mRNA.
abstract: Anticancer peptides (ACPs) offer a promising alternative to conventional chemotherapy but face challenges, including poor selectivity, limited tumor penetration, low cellular uptake, and rapid degradation in serum. To address these barriers, we developed synthetic mRNAs encoding chimeric ACPs designed for enhanced intracellular delivery and activity. mRNAs for constructs SAK6L9AS(1X), SAK6L9AS(4X), and WTAS-K6L9(4X) were transcribed in vitro and tested against 4T1 breast cancer cells. Cytotoxicity was assessed by cell confluence and MTT assays, while apoptosis was evaluated using caspase 3/7 activation, PI staining, and Annexin V flow cytometry. Our results demonstrate that all SAK6L9AS variants induced robust apoptosis and cellular toxicity in 4T1 cells. Importantly, this work provides the first demonstration of intracellular expression of an mRNA-encoded ACP fused to a cell-penetrating peptide, thereby validating a modular platform for RNA-based delivery of anticancer agents. This study highlights the feasibility of mRNA-encoded peptide therapeutics as a scalable and customizable strategy for cancer treatment. By combining the advantages of mRNA delivery with rational peptide design, ACP chimeras can be expressed directly inside tumor cells, overcoming the limitations of exogenous peptide administration. Our findings support further development of synthetic mRNA therapeutics to generate potent, selective anticancer peptides with reduced systemic toxicity and improved translational potential.

title: Cloning, Expression and Functionality Evaluation of Recombinant Monoclonal Antibody Against VP1 Capsid Protein of FMD Virus.
abstract: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) is a highly contagious viral disease caused by the FMD virus (FMDV), which belongs to the Aphthovirus genus in the Picornaviridae family. FMDV is a highly variable RNA virus, and there is limited cross-protection between serotypes and strains. The disease can have devastating economic, social, and environmental impacts. The FMDV capsid is composed of VP1-VP4 structural proteins, with VP1 being the most abundant protein consisting of 213 amino acids. The G-H loop (residues 141-160) of the VP1 capsid protein is highly variable and serves as the main antigenic region. It contains a conserved triplet of amino acids, Arg-Gly-Asp (RGD), which induces the production of protective antibodies against various FMDV types. Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) play a crucial role in detecting and serotyping FMDV in pathological samples, as well as evaluating protection post-vaccination against FMD. This study explores the expression and function of an engineered recombinant single-chain variable fragment (scFv-mAb) in Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3) Rosetta strain as a cost-effective prokaryotic system with high yield. The scFv-mAb gene was inserted into the pET28a (+) expression plasmid. E. coli cells were transformed with the plasmid, induced with 0.5 mM IPTG, and incubated at 37 ˚C for 12 hours. The protein was purified using a Ni2+-NTA resin column and analyzed by 12% SDS-PAGE for quality assessment. The efficiency and functionality of the scFv-mAb were confirmed using an indirect sandwich (capture) enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). The purified scFv-mAb concentration was determined to be approximately 2.00 mg/mL using the Bradford assay under optimal conditions. Each well was coated with 400 ng of scFv-mAb based on checkerboard results and the mean of negative serum at a 1:10 dilution. The indirect sandwich ELISA assay yielded an optical density (OD) signal range of 0.3 to 1.5 at a 450 nm wavelength in different positive control treatments. The ELISA results showed that the scFv-mAb fragment successfully detected serotype O of FMDV. Further research could confirm the potential of this recombinant antibody for broader commercial applications in the future.

title: Mapping the subcellular pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic landscape: a systems-pharmacology framework for predicting combination therapies against intracellular bacterial infections.
abstract: Intracellular bacterial pathogens represent one of the most formidable challenges in contemporary medicine. By exploiting host cellular niches, these organisms evade immune surveillance and withstand conventional antibiotic therapies, establishing persistent reservoirs that are difficult to eradicate. Although antibiotic combinations, host-directed interventions, and drug repurposing have shown promise, conventional discovery pipelines rarely capture the dynamic and compartmentalized nature of the intracellular environment. This review proposes a systems pharmacology framework centered on subcellular pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (Sub-PK/PD) profiling to predict and optimize intracellular combination therapies. Mechanistic and translational studies of intracellular drug disposition, host-pathogen metabolism, computational combination design, and biomimetic infection models were synthesized in a targeted narrative review. Particular attention was given to spatially resolved measurements, dual ribonucleic acid (RNA) sequencing, metabolic flux analysis, machine learning, and organ-on-a-chip platforms. Pathogen-containing vacuoles, phagolysosomes, the host cytosol, lipid-rich macrophages, and tissue lesions impose distinct barriers to drug ionization, accumulation, stability, and target engagement. Persistent infection also produces reciprocal metabolic rewiring: host pathways supply carbon, nitrogen, lipids, metals, and reducing equivalents, while bacterial stress programs alter growth and antibiotic susceptibility. Integrating these processes can reveal shared metabolic bottlenecks suitable for combinations of pathogen-directed and host-directed agents. Computational models can prioritize combinations, but their predictions require validation under physiologically realistic concentration-time profiles. Linking systems biology to localized Sub-PK/PD provides a practical roadmap for designing niche-specific regimens. Such regimens could improve clearance of persistent intracellular reservoirs, reduce ineffective exposure, and limit the emergence of antimicrobial resistance.

title: The human circular Tau 12->7 RNA is translated in mouse neurons and promotes tau aggregation.
abstract: In addition to numerous mRNA isoforms, the human microtubule associated protein tau ( MAPT ) gene generates circular RNAs that are not known to be expressed in rodents. Using adeno associated viruses, we expressed human circular Tau RNA generated from backsplicing of exon 12 to exon 7 (circTau 12->7) in mouse brain. We observed rolling circle translation of circTau 12->7, similar to cultured human HEK293 cells. Despite using a ubiquitously active promoter, circTau 12->7 protein and a control circEGFP protein were only observed in mouse neurons, indicating neuron-specific translation of these circular RNAs. CircTau 12->7 expression resulted in tau aggregates resembling neurofibrillary tangles in mouse brain that included endogenous mouse tau protein. Our data support a model where neuron-specific translation of circTau RNAs induces 'linear' mRNA-translated tau aggregation, which could contribute to tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease. Thus, targeting circTau RNAs could be a therapeutic approach for Alzheimer's disease.

title: Hydrogel dimensionality directs mechanics-dependent nascent matrix deposition by tendon fibroblasts.
abstract: Tendon fibroblasts continuously synthesize and remodel extracellular matrix (ECM) in response to their surrounding mechanical environment in vivo and in vitro , yet how dimensionality regulates the deposition of newly synthesized matrix remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated nascent matrix deposition by primary mouse tail tendon fibroblasts cultured on flat two-dimensional (2D) or encapsulated within three-dimensional (3D) norbornene-modified hyaluronic acid hydrogels with tunable mechanical properties. Newly synthesized matrix was visualized using metabolic labeling with azido-galactosamine (GalNAz), which labels nascent glycoproteins deposited during culture. In 2D, increasing hydrogel elastic modulus from 10 to 25 kPa enhanced nascent matrix deposition. This response was accompanied by increased cell spreading and YAP nuclear localization, indicating increased cellular mechanosensing. In contrast, tendon fibroblasts encapsulated within enzymatically degradable 3D hydrogels showed progressive matrix deposition over time but deposited less nascent matrix in stiffer (∼50 kPa) hydrogels compared with softer 5 and 10 kPa hydrogels. YAP nuclear localization was increased in softer hydrogels compared with 50 kPa hydrogels. Bulk RNA sequencing showed increased expression of tendon matrisome-associated genes in softer 3D hydrogels, including increased tenascin C and collagen type I expression. These findings demonstrate that hydrogel dimensionality determines the relationship between matrix mechanics and nascent matrix deposition. This work establishes a framework for studying how engineered microenvironments regulate the matrix-producing behavior of tendon fibroblasts and provides insight into the design of biomaterials for investigating tendon biology and matrix remodeling.

title: Structures of MyD88 and its oncogenic mutant reveal DNA binding with implications for cytosolic DNA sensing.
abstract: MyD88 is a universal adaptor that connects to Toll-like receptors and interleukin-1 receptors through its Toll/IL-1R homology (TIR) domain and activates inflammatory signaling via its death domain (DD). However, how MyD88 TIR serves as the platform for these functions and if it has additional functions remain unclear. Here, we report cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of MyD88 TIR and its cancer-specific mutant L252P (previously L265P) mainly in ring and spiral forms, respectively. Both assemblies are formed by antiparallel double-filaments, using canonical TIR interfaces within each strand but unique surfaces between the strands, and position MyD88 DD at the same sides of the assemblies for self-oligomerization and pathway activation. Surprisingly, these WT or L252P filaments are bound to dsDNA using the concave sides of the rings and the spirals. In vitro assays and cellular studies establish that MyD88 directly binds dsDNA and promotes inflammatory cytokine expression, particularly pro-IL-1β, following dsDNA transfection or viral infection. Notably, these responses are unaffected by deficiency of UNC93B1, the essential chaperone required for trafficking endosomal nucleic acid-sensing TLRs. Structure-guide MyD88 mutant that disrupts dsDNA binding specifically compromises dsDNA-induced transcriptional program while maintaining TLR signaling. RNA-seq further reveals that MyD88 plays a crucial role in inducing gene expression upon dsDNA sensing and that about half of cGAS-dependent genes are also MyD88-dependent. Together, our structural, biochemical and genetic data support the findings that MyD88 directly engages with cytosolic dsDNA and cooperates with cGAS to promote the full innate immune transcriptional response.

title: An Enzyme-Mediated Duplex Exponential Amplification Assay for Rapid Detection of Plasmodiophora brassicae.
abstract: Clubroot, caused by the soilborne obligate biotrophic protist Plasmodiophora brassicae, substantially reduces the yield and quality of cruciferous crops worldwide. In this study, an enzyme-mediated duplex exponential amplification (EmDEA) assay was developed for rapid detection of P. brassicae in extracted DNA. By comparing the P. brassicae strain 3A genome with representative bacterial, fungal, and oomycete genome assemblies, we identified 157 candidate regions that showed no detectable matches in the selected non-target genomes under the specified alignment criteria. Pbspec1, a fragment within the annotated locus PBTT_08698, was selected based on computational non-target screening, within-species conservation, and suitability for assay design. PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing were used to validate the target fragment. Six forward primers, six reverse primers, and six RNA probes were screened, and F2-R4-RNA2 was selected for subsequent EmDEA experiments. Using serial dilutions of purified recombinant plasmid DNA, the F2-R4-RNA2 combination consistently detected template concentrations of 1.0 × 103 copies/μL and above. No amplification was observed from the 12 non-target fungal or bacterial organisms. The assay detected P. brassicae in DNA extracted from four infected root samples and three naturally infested soil samples. All tested positive samples produced detectable fluorescence during a programmed 20-min run on a portable isothermal fluorescence instrument. These results support the potential use of EmDEA for rapid preliminary screening of P. brassicae following DNA extraction.

title: Characterization of the organelle genomes of mycoheterotrophic Thismia angustimitra and evidence suggesting horizontal gene transfer.
abstract: Our knowledge about mitochondrial genome evolution in plants is lacking far behind our knowledge of plastome evolution. In heterotrophic plants, it is well-known that plastome degradation and reduced or lost photosynthesis go hand in hand, and there is little if any difference between plastome evolution in mycoheterotrophic and haustorial parasites. The mitochondrial genome appears less affected by a heterotrophic lifestyle, although exceptions occur. In contrast to plastome evolution, mitochondrial evolution may differ between mycoheterotrophic and haustorial parasites, in particular with regards to the occurrence of horizontal gene transfer. However, data from mycoheterotrophs are scarce, and complete mitogenomes are only known from three of ten clades. Here we present data from the complete plastome and mitogenome from Thismia angustimitra, representing a fourth clade of mycoheterotrophs. The 18,215 bp plastome is much reduced and includes only few genes. The mitogenome has a multicircular structure consisting of 22 chromosomes with a total length of 422,400 bp. The gene content and the pattern of RNA editing are normal. The mitogenome includes only few repeats and recombinational activity is limited. A search for foreign DNA did not reveal any fungal sequences, the content of plastid DNA is low, but a large proportion of intergenic DNA shows similarity to distantly related angiosperms. Just a few plastid inserts appear to have originated through intracellular transfer, whereas others most likely stem from horizontal gene transfer. Synteny patterns of the intergenic sequences suggest that horizontal transfer may happen in either direction. The highly reduced plastome of T. angustimitra fits completely the general picture of plastome degradation in heterotrophic plants. Whereas the mitogenome in many aspects appears unaffected by the lifestyle, the recombinational activity is unusually low. Surprisingly, we find evidence suggesting horizontal gene transfer, indicating that this phenomenon may be more common among mycoheterotrophic plants than previously thought.

title: PRKAG2 Cardiac Syndrome: A Comprehensive Review of Clinical Manifestations, Pathophysiological Mechanisms, and Precision Medicine Frontiers.
abstract: PRKAG2 cardiac syndrome (PCS) is a metabolic storage cardiomyopathy caused by pathogenic variants in the PRKAG2 gene encoding the γ2-subunit of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK). It is defined by left ventricular hypertrophy, ventricular preexcitation and progressive conduction system disease accompanied by early-onset atrial arrhythmias. This review systematically evaluates PCS, outlining its clinical manifestations, genotype-phenotype spectrum, and diagnostic clues that distinguish it from sarcomeric hypertrophy. It explores underlying pathophysiological mechanisms, detailing how chronic AMPK activation drives glycogen accumulation via allosteric G6P activation of glycogen synthase, following a biphasic temporal model from early GLUT4-mediated glucose flooding to late metabolic feedback suppression. It further examines how Akt-mTOR hyperactivation fosters hypertrophy and how activated fasciculoventricular pathways mediate preexcitation. Finally, it reviews current supportive clinical management and highlights emerging precision medicine frontiers-including RNA-based silencing, pharmacological pathway inhibitors, and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing-that aim to shift PCS care toward targeted disease modification.

title: A universal twist-slide coupling mechanism governs deformations of DNA, RNA, and RNA-DNA hybrid duplexes.
abstract: Nucleic acid duplexes, including DNA, RNA, and RNA-DNA hybrid (RDH), undergo structural deformations that are essential for genome replication, transcription, and RNA-mediated regulation. However, quantitative measurements and mechanistic understanding of these deformations remain limited. Here, we probe nucleic acid deformations by measuring helical twist changes using single-molecule magnetic tweezers, where minute twist variations ( ~ 0.01° per base pair) accumulate over kilobase-length duplexes and become experimentally detectable. Unexpectedly, we find that RDHs do not behave as a simple intermediate between DNA and RNA. Instead, RDHs exhibit markedly attenuated twist responses to salt and temperature, together with nearly vanishing twist-stretch coupling. Despite these distinct mechanical behaviors, all-atom molecular dynamics simulations reveal a common deformation pathway shared by all three duplex types: external perturbations first modulate base-pair slide, which is subsequently transduced into twist changes through a universal twist-slide coupling. Building on this mechanism, we derive approximate theoretical predictions that quantitatively reproduce the salt- and temperature-dependent twist responses of RDH. We further show that protein-induced RDH deformations also occur predominantly along the twist-slide coupling pathway. Together, our results establish twist-slide coupling as a universal framework governing nucleic acid deformations across duplex types and environmental conditions.

title: Inhibition of Ptbp1 in microglia alleviates neuroinflammation by the Cbx5-Ifitm3 axis.
abstract: Polypyrimidine tract-binding protein 1 (Ptbp1) is a member of the heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins that govern numerous aspects of the messenger RNA life cycle, including splicing, stability, and translation. This study investigated its role in cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) with a focus on microglia. A model of transient middle cerebral artery occlusion in mice and an oxygen-glucose deprivation/reperfusion (OGD/R) model in mouse BV2 cells were used. Ptbp1 was significantly upregulated in microglia following CIRI. Inhibition of Ptbp1 attenuated the inflammatory response in BV2 cells and reduced damage to co-cultured neurons under OGD/R conditions; it also reduced tissue inflammation, mitigated brain tissue damage, and improved neurological function on days 1, 3 and 7 after reperfusion in vivo. Mechanistically, Ptbp1 destabilized chromobox protein homolog 5 (Cbx5), thereby attenuating Cbx5/Suv39h1-mediated H3K9me3 enrichment and transcriptional repression at the interferon-induced transmembrane protein 3 (Ifitm3) promoter, promoting Ifitm3 expression and enhancing Tlr4/p65 signaling. The regulation of Cbx5 mRNA stability by Ptbp1 and the inhibitory effect of Cbx5 on Ifitm3 were also confirmed in IMG cells. The present findings suggest that Ptbp1 reduces the stability of Cbx5 mRNA, thereby attenuating Cbx5/Suv39h1-mediated transcriptional repression of Ifitm3, enhancing Tlr4/p65 signaling and the inflammatory response, and exacerbating neuronal damage and CIRI.

title: CircRNA9389 inhibits NKRF nuclear translocation to activate the NFκB pathway and upregulate PD-L1 expression promoting colorectal cancer progression.
abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) play a crucial role in regulating the progression of various cancers and the cancer immune microenvironment. However, the molecular mechanisms how the circRNAs influence colorectal cancer (CRC) development and tumor immune remain to be thoroughly explored and elucidated. We identified a novel CRC-associated circRNA (circRNA9389) through high-throughput sequencing. The circular structure of circRNA9389 was confirmed using Sanger sequencing and DNA electrophoresis with convergent and divergent primers. Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) was employed to explore the expression of circRNA9389 in cancerous and adjacent tissues and its correlation with PD-L1 expression. CRC cells and animal models were utilized to assess the effects of circRNA9389 on CRC proliferation and metastasis. Western blotting (WB), RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP), chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP), and dual-luciferase reporter assays were conducted to explore the mechanisms by which circRNA9389 promotes CRC progression and PD-L1 expression. CircRNA9389 was derived from Aspartate Beta-Hydroxylase (ASPH) gene, and significantly upregulated in CRC tissues, with high expression levels correlating with advanced TNM stage. A strong positive correlation was observed between circRNA9389 and PD-L1 mRNA expression. Overexpression of circRNA9389 promoted CRC cell proliferation, metastasis, and invasion, while its inhibition had the opposite effects. Mechanistically, circRNA9389 bound to the non-canonical nuclear localization signal (NLS) of the R3H domain of NKRF protein, thereby blocking its nuclear translocation, activating the NF-κB signaling pathway, and upregulating PD-L1 expression. Additionally, p65 in the NF-κB pathway bound to the P2 promoter region of the ASPH gene to enhance the synthesis of circRNA9389. Our study identifies a novel circRNA (circRNA9389), and reveals the mechanisms for circRNA9389 promoting CRC progression. Collectively, circRNA9389 might be a novel therapeutic target for CRC.

title: High-dose parecoxib induces stress-associated pathological remodeling in C2C12 myotubes.
abstract: Parecoxib is a selective COX-2 inhibitor widely used for postoperative analgesia. Although NSAIDs can influence cellular metabolism and stress responses, whether parecoxib alters skeletal muscle cell homeostasis has not been systematically examined. Here, differentiated C2C12 myotubes were used as an in vitro model to investigate parecoxib-induced stress remodeling. Parecoxib caused limited changes in myotube morphology at 1 and 4 μM, whereas significant structural changes were observed at 10, 50, and 100 μM compared with control. Protein-normalized ATP content was reduced, whereas LDH release was not increased across the tested concentration range. Parecoxib also reduced Akt and FoxO3a phosphorylation, increased atrogin-1 and Bax expression, and increased AMPK phosphorylation. RNA sequencing identified changes in Gadd45a, Hmox1, Tnfaip3, Depp1, Tfrc, and Abra. Functional enrichment analyses highlighted pathways related to PI3K-Akt, FoxO, MAPK, cytoskeletal organization, muscle differentiation, and myofibril assembly. Parecoxib exposure during differentiation produced limited changes at 1 and 4 μM, whereas significant impairment was observed at 10, 50, and 100 μM compared with control. Together the results show structural and stress-related changes in C2C12 myotubes at higher parecoxib concentrations. They do not establish skeletal muscle toxicity under clinical exposure conditions.

title: Synthesis of Ovarian Cancer Multi-Omics Datasets: A Biology-Informed Evaluation Framework
abstract: Paired multi-omic cancer cohorts are costly to assemble and difficult to share, motivating synthetic cohorts as a complementary resource. As generative model development accelerates, we shift the focus from proposing yet another architecture to defining evaluation criteria that determine whether synthetic data preserve biologically relevant structure. We introduce a biology-informed and patient-disjoint framework for evaluating the generation of paired RNA expression and copy-number variation (CNV) profiles, and apply it to the longitudinal DECIDER high-grade serous ovarian cancer cohort. The framework assesses modality-specific fidelity and coherence between RNA and CNV pairs using agreement between real training and held-out data as a reference, alongside complementary training-data proximity diagnostics. We adapt three multi-omic integration architectures based on variational autoencoders to generate paired profiles. The model leading several fidelity and coherence measures also shows the strongest training-data proximity. The protocol and case study offer the community a reference for comparing future multi-omic generators.

title: Yellow fever virus infection triggers the assembly of compositionally unique and specialised stress granules.
abstract: The phase separation of biomolecules into stress granules (SGs) allows the cell to tightly regulate translation activity in response to different stimuli, such as oxidative stress, starvation, or the recognition of non-cellular RNA. Recent reports suggest SGs induced during viral infection may act as a crossroad between the cellular stress response and the activation of the innate immune response. Here, we aimed to dissect the role of SGs in the context of yellow fever virus (YFV) infection. We found that YFV infection with both 17D vaccine and Asibi pathogenic strains resulted in translational shut-off and the formation of SGs at 48 hours post infection (hpi), although viral infection was already apparent at 24 hpi. This delay may be coupled to the ability of the YFV capsid to inhibit SG formation through an interaction with the SG scaffolding protein G3BP1. To elucidate the role of YFV-induced SGs during infection, we inhibited SG assembly using a small-molecule inhibitor as well as siRNA-mediated knockdown of SGs and found that while SG formation does not impact viral replication, silencing of SG scaffolding proteins is associated with increased expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISG). Uncovering the proteome of YFV-induced SGs, our compositional analysis revealed a unique composition, distinct from NaAs-induced SGs, which displayed enrichment in mitochondrial proteins. Further functional analysis revealed that YFV infection is associated with mitochondrial damage and dysfunction, which coincides with formation of virus-induced SGs. Together, we propose that YFV-induced SGs may be involved not only in the modulation of cellular homeostasis but also in influencing mitochondrial functions.

title: USP18 deubiquitylates TRIM25 to facilitate RIG-I-mediated antiviral innate immune signaling.
abstract: The cytosolic sensor retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I) is essential for initiating antiviral innate immunity, and its activation is tightly regulated by ubiquitination. Although the deubiquitinating enzyme ubiquitin-specific protease 18 (USP18) is known to regulate interferon signaling, its role in the RIG-I pathway remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that USP18 acts as a positive regulator of RIG-I-mediated antiviral responses. We find that USP18 specifically promotes K63-linked ubiquitination of endogenous RIG-I during viral infection, potentiates downstream interferon signaling, and restricts RNA virus replication. Mechanistically, USP18 directly binds to the E3 ligase tripartite motif-containing 25 (TRIM25) and removes its K48-linked ubiquitin chains primarily at lysine 156 (K156), thereby stabilizing the TRIM25 protein. This deubiquitinating activity is essential, as a catalytic mutant (USP18 C64S) binds TRIM25 but fails to stabilize it or enhance RIG-I signaling. Knockdown of TRIM25 abolishes USP18-mediated enhancement of RIG-I ubiquitination and the interferon response, establishing that TRIM25 is required for USP18-mediated enhancement. Our study unveils a novel USP18-TRIM25-RIG-I axis that amplifies antiviral immunity, revealing USP18 as a multifaceted regulator that fine-tunes interferon responses at both the receptor and sensor levels.

title: GCN5L1 Depletion Promotes Left Ventricular Fibrosis in Failing Hearts via Upregulation of RAB7A.
abstract: Pathologic cardiac fibrosis is one of the key determinants of adverse remodeling and progression to heart failure. Although GCN5-like 1 (GCN5L1) is documented to regulate cardiac metabolic homeostasis, its role in myocardial remodeling and fibrosis is unknown. In a murine transverse aortic constriction (TAC) pressure overload model, GCN5L1 protein abundance was significantly reduced in the left ventricular (LV) tissues from wild type (WT) mice. This finding was concurrent with increased collagen 1α1 expression in the same tissues. Interestingly, LVs from cardiomyocyte-specific GCN5L1 knockout (GCN5L1 cKO) mice showed exacerbated TAC-induced collagen 1α1 expression among profibrotic genes identified by bulk RNA sequencing, when compared with corresponding WT mice. These finding are consistent with our previous report of increased fibrotic tissue and decreased fractional shortening (a marker of contractile function) in GCN5L1 cKO mice under TAC stress. Consistently, analysis of human hearts with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction demonstrated reduced GCN5L1 expression accompanied by increased collagen 1α1, revealing a conserved inverse relationship. In vitro, we further demonstrate that conditioned media collected from GCN5L1-depleted AC16 human ventricular cardiomyocyte-like cells induced upregulation of collagen 1α1 expression in human cardiac fibroblasts. Proteomic profiling of WT and GCN5L1 cKO cardiac tissues aligned with our in vitro findings in WT and GCN5L1 knockout (KO) mouse embryonic fibroblasts, revealing increased expression of lysosomal, endo-lysosomal, and autophagy markers (including RAB7A) in response to GCN5L1 deficiency. In vivo, RAB7A protein was increased following TAC, which was exacerbated in GCN5L1-deficient hearts under the same conditions. Furthermore, in human ventricular fibroblasts, TGF-β1 stimulated RAB7A and collagen 1α1 expression. Importantly, RAB7A knockdown attenuated TGF-β1-induced collagen 1α1, whereas GCN5L1 knockdown altered expression of fibrosis related markers and increased RAB7A without directly altering collagen expression. Collectively, these findings identify GCN5L1 as a negative regulator of pressure overload-induced cardiac fibrosis, and implicate a GCN5L1- RAB7A axis linking lysosomal pathways to collagen deposition in ventricular remodeling. These findings highlight a potential therapeutic target to attenuate LV fibrosis.

title: Silencing hepatic complement factor B inhibits alternative pathway activation and attenuates arthritis in CAIA model.
abstract: The complement system comprises tightly regulated enzymatic cascades that are essential for innate immune defense and tissue homeostasis. Although protective under physiological conditions, complement dysregulation can drive inflammation and tissue injury and contributes to the pathogenesis of autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, prompting the development of complement-targeted therapies. Here, we describe the development and nonclinical evaluation of AZD6912, a GalNAc-conjugated small interfering RNA (siRNA) designed to silence hepatic complement factor B (CFB) as a potential treatment for rheumatoid arthritis. AZD6912 produced potent on-target knockdown of CFB in a hepatocyte cell line and a primary human hepatocyte spheroid model, with no evidence of off-target effects. In mice, a surrogate siRNA targeting hepatic Cfb achieved >90% reduction in liver Cfb mRNA and >95% reduction in circulating CFB protein. This target-specific silencing reduced local complement production, attenuated joint inflammation, and provided therapeutic benefit in the collagen antibody-induced arthritis (CAIA) model. In non-human primates, AZD6912 showed high hepatic exposure, >80% suppression of hepatic CFB mRNA, sustained reductions in serum CFB, and >95% inhibition of complement activity. Safety assessments were unremarkable. Collectively, these findings demonstrate durable siRNA-mediated silencing of CFB with downstream pharmacologic and therapeutic effects, support the clinical development of AZD6912, and highlight the potential of GalNAc-siRNA therapeutics in immune-mediated diseases.

title: SUMOylation counteracts ubiquitination to stabilize ANKRD1 and promote osimertinib resistance in lung adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Acquired resistance to osimertinib remains a major challenge in the treatment of EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), yet the contribution of stress-responsive protein homeostasis to resistance remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to investigate the role and regulatory mechanisms of ankyrin repeat domain 1 (ANKRD1) in acquired osimertinib resistance. Public transcriptomic datasets and machine learning-based feature selection were integrated with osimertinib-resistant LUAD cell models, paired clinical specimens, RNA sequencing, biochemical and molecular assays, functional rescue experiments, and in vivo tumor models to investigate the role of ANKRD1 and its upstream and downstream regulatory mechanisms in osimertinib resistance. ANKRD1 was upregulated in osimertinib-resistant LUAD models and promoted tumor cell survival under therapeutic pressure. Mechanistically, zinc finger protein 593 (ZNF593) interacted with ANKRD1 and facilitated its SUMO1-dependent modification, which was associated with reduced ubiquitin-mediated degradation and enhanced ANKRD1 protein stability. Stabilized ANKRD1 subsequently promoted MERTK expression and sustained downstream AKT signaling, thereby supporting tumor cell survival under osimertinib pressure. Furthermore, K41 emerged as a critical regulatory residue, as K41R simultaneously impaired ANKRD1 SUMOylation, ubiquitination, and interaction with ZNF593, accompanied by attenuated downstream signaling and resistance phenotypes. These findings suggest that K41 plays an important role in coordinating ANKRD1 post-translational regulation and its interaction with ZNF593. Our study identifies a proteostasis-related mechanism contributing to acquired osimertinib resistance and provides mechanistic insight into the ZNF593-ANKRD1-MERTK axis in EGFR-mutant LUAD. These findings support further investigation of this regulatory axis as a potential vulnerability in osimertinib-resistant LUAD.

title: Detection of N 3-methylcytidine in RNA at single base resolution using Protoscript II to read through and generate high mutation rates.
abstract: N 3-methylcytidine (m3C), an RNA modification involving methylation of cytidine at the Watson-Crick-Franklin edge, has been identified in human tRNA, mitochondrial tRNA (mt-tRNA), and mRNA. In tRNA and mt-tRNA, it has been shown to play important roles in tRNA structure and translation. Here we describe a new approach which utilizes the high readthrough and mutation rates of Protoscript II (PSII) at m3C sites in combination with AlkB demethylation to detect m3C at single-base resolution. We first validate the method on synthetic probes. Then, using this method, we successfully identify known m3C sites on tRNA and mt-tRNA, as well as one new candidate tRNA m3C site. We further show that none of the m3C sites identified in cytosolic tRNA are likely METTL8 substrates. In contrast, the two m3C sites detected in mt-tRNA are sensitive to METTL8 knockdown (KD) and over expression (OE), in line with their previous characterization as METTL8 substrates. These results demonstrate that our method can be used to investigate changes in the m3C level in many sites using an unbiased approach. Overall, this study introduces a convenient high-resolution method for m3C mapping with high readthrough rates, paving the way for future mechanistic studies on the biological function of m3C and its effector proteins.

title: Harnessing metatranscriptomics to unveil the metabolic landscape of microbiota in traditional fermented foods.
abstract: Traditional fermented foods are widely consumed and valued for their distinctive sensory properties and potential health benefits. These foods contain complex microbiota whose interactions and metabolic activities shape biochemical transformations relevant to product quality, safety, and functionality. Metatranscriptomics provides a culture-independent means of profiling community RNA and examining changes in microbial gene expression during fermentation. However, most fermented-food microbiome studies continue to infer function from community composition or genomic potential rather than from in situ gene expression. Existing metatranscriptomic applications also differ substantially in sampling, RNA processing, sequencing, and data analysis, limiting comparisons across food systems. This review examines the metatranscriptomic workflows applied to fermented foods, including sample preparation, sequencing strategies, and bioinformatic analysis. It identifies practical requirements for reproducible RNA-based studies in complex food matrices and compares transcriptionally represented taxa and pathways across fermentation systems. The review also distinguishes gene expression from realized metabolic activity, an important boundary when interpreting transcript annotations and reconstructed pathways. We further assess the strengths and limitations of metatranscriptomics, both alone and in combination with complementary omics, for resolving microbiota structure-function relationships. Key challenges include data integration, evidence interpretation, and the recovery of biologically meaningful information from complex transcriptomic datasets. When combined with complementary omics and experimental validation, metatranscriptomics can help relate expressed genes and pathways to fermentation phenotypes. These insights may guide the experimental evaluation of starter cultures and the development of more precise fermentation-control strategies.

title: The regulator of G protein signaling RGS9 supports insulin secretion in male mouse islets.
abstract: Regulators of G protein signaling (RGS) proteins terminate G protein-coupled receptor signaling and regulate multiple aspects of pancreatic islet function. Although RGS9 is highly enriched in human and rodent islets, its cellular localization and physiological role remain largely unknown. Here, we investigated the expression of Rgs9 in mouse islets and its contribution to insulin secretion. Rgs9 expression was characterized by RNA in situ hybridization and fluorescence-activated cell sorting coupled with quantitative PCR. Rgs9 function was investigated by shRNA-mediated knockdown in wild-type and Dishevelled, Egl-10 and Pleckstrin (DEP) domain-deficient Rgs9 mutant ( Rgs9 ΔDEP/ΔDEP ) mouse pseudo-islets. Rgs9 was detected throughout the endocrine pancreas but was enriched in β and δ cells, with the Rgs9-1 isoform representing the predominant splice variant in mouse islets. Rgs9 knockdown in mouse pseudo-islets impaired glucose- and KCl-stimulated insulin secretion without affecting insulin content. In contrast, Rgs9 ΔDEP/ΔDEP mouse islets failed to reproduce this phenotype. Further characterization of the mutant mice revealed persistent expression of Rgs9 transcripts, which when knocked down impaired both glucose- and KCl-stimulated insulin secretion. These data indicate that RGS9 supports glucose-stimulated insulin secretion. Given that RGS9 acts exclusively on Gαi/o, our results further suggest that RGS9 in β cells dampens inhibitory signaling to promote insulin secretion. Finally, the Rgs9 ΔDEP/ΔDEP mutant does not represent a complete loss-of-function in islets likely due to the retention of the GTPase-activating protein (GAP) activity in the absence of the DEP domain.

title: SERPINE1 Identifies a Shared Injury-associated Molecular Signature in Intracerebral Hemorrhage and Epilepsy.
abstract: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) and epilepsy are clinically linked neurological disorders, yet their shared molecular features remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to identify shared molecular candidates across ICH and epilepsy by integrating transcriptomic data with a curated set of genes with established circadian relevance. Transcriptomic datasets for ICH and epilepsy were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus, and candidate genes were curated from the Molecular Signatures Database and GeneCards. Differentially expressed candidate genes were intersected, and an integrative machine-learning framework-including Boruta, LASSO, XGBoost, and CatBoost-was applied to prioritize shared genes. Integrated machine-learning and network analyses nominated SERPINE1 for further investigation. Single-sample gene set enrichment analysis identified higher scores for porphyrin, folate and pterine, and arachidonic acid metabolism in both disease comparisons. SERPINE1 expression correlated positively with arachidonic acid metabolism scores in both datasets, while Hallmark gene set enrichment analysis linked its expression to inflammatory transcriptional signatures, including TNFA signaling via NFKB and IL6-JAK-STAT3 signaling. Gene interaction, drug-mRNA, transcription factor-mRNA, and competing endogenous RNA networks further characterized its regulatory and pharmacological context. Independent bulk transcriptomic datasets and experimental models supported SERPINE1 upregulation, with single-nucleus RNA-sequencing providing complementary cellular context, while single-nucleus analyses and immunostaining further supported its preferential microglial localization. Collectively, these findings identify SERPINE1 as a shared injury-associated molecular feature of ICH and epilepsy, with preferential microglial localization and associations with inflammatory transcriptional signatures and metabolic pathway scores. Although SERPINE1 is known to be clock-regulated, whether its temporal expression pattern is altered in ICH or epilepsy remains to be determined.

title: Reconstructing the human enhancer RNA transcriptome.
abstract: Transcript-resolved models of RNA enable functional interrogation of RNA biology by linking processing, structure, localisation, and regulatory interactions to specific RNA molecules. Across coding and noncoding transcriptomes, such models have been essential for defining RNA-level mechanisms relevant to physiology and disease. Enhancer RNAs (eRNAs), however, remain largely uncharacterised without transcript-level definitions, and no widely adopted transcript-resolved reference exists, limiting investigation of how individual eRNAs are processed, localised, and participate in transcriptional regulation or their emerging post-transcriptional functions. Here, we reconstruct a transcript-resolved catalogue of stable human eRNAs by pan-transcriptome assembly across diverse tissues, cell types, and compartments, defining 36,536 transcripts, including a subset with multi-exonic structures. We demonstrate that eRNA splice junctions are reproducible features that exhibit cell-type bias, subcellular localisation bias, and sensitivity to spliceosome perturbation. In perturbation experiments, eRNA splice junction usage responded to SF3B1 mutation, nuclear-cytoplasmic partitioning, and pharmacological inhibition of RNA export, demonstrating regulation across multiple layers of RNA biology. In head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, a subset of these junctions showed altered usage between tumour and matched normal tissue, indicating that processing varies in disease contexts. Across three validation contexts, nearly one-fifth of reconstructed junctions were detectable, with some showing regulated usage, supporting biological reproducibility. Motivated by these observations, we provide both the GTF annotation and junctions BED file, as a framework for studying stable eRNAs, enabling RNA-centric investigation of their potential functions. The annotations have been incorporated into the eRNAkit database, available at https://github.com/AneneLab/eRNAkit .

title: Hidden diversity from transposable element RNAs in cancer.
abstract: In this issue of Molecular Cell, Li et al.1 define TEtrans, a class of RNA transcripts that initiate and splice between transposable elements independent of host genes. Mining population-scale transcriptome databases, they uncover a widespread, tumor-enriched repertoire of protein-coding and non-coding TEtrans associated with cancer outcomes.

title: EGFP Reporter Assay in Transgenic Zebrafish Embryos for Assessing Formulation-Dependent dsRNA Bioavailability.
abstract: RNA interference (RNAi) is a sequence-specific gene silencing mechanism increasingly exploited for the development of sprayable, species-selective pest control products. For many applications, the trigger molecule double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) must be stabilized via suitable formulation strategies to ensure delivery to the target site and enable biological activity. Currently, there is no standardized approach to assess dsRNA bioavailability as a function of its formulation in fish. However, this is a critical step in assessing the environmental risks posed by formulated dsRNA to fish and other non-target organisms. Here, we present a zebrafish embryo-based assay using the Tg(fli1:EGFP)y1 reporter line to assess dsRNA bioavailability by quantifying RNAi-mediated gene silencing. Based on OECD Test Guideline 236, zebrafish embryos are exposed to sublethal concentrations of nano-lipid formulated dsRNA designed to target the EGFP messenger RNA (mRNA). After 96 h of exposure via immersion, embryos are either assessed microscopically or homogenized to quantify EGFP signal, providing a rapid, high-throughput readout without the need for dissection or individual embryo handling. EGFP downregulation at the protein level, analyzed by fluorescence signal quantification, is complemented by quantifying EGFP mRNA levels using RT-qPCR. Representative results show a concentration-dependent reduction of EGFP signal along with decreased EGFP transcript levels, indicating effective uptake and functional delivery of the nano-lipid formulated dsRNA. This workflow provides a reliable method for assessing the cellular bioavailability of dsRNA as a function of its formulation. Additionally, the microplate reader-based fluorescence measurement offers a straightforward and time-efficient readout, reducing animal use. Utilizing zebrafish embryos, the method is furthermore a refined approach, reducing the need for experiments on protected life stages of fish, supporting the 3Rs principle. More broadly, this protocol is adaptable for additional applications, including the modification of the reporter line, target gene, or nanoparticle-based delivery system for use in developmental and (eco‑)toxicological studies.

title: Profiling of RNA 8-oxoG marks in Escherichia coli identifies critical intrinsic characteristics that contribute to 8-oxoG accumulation in bacteria.
abstract: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are environmentally ubiquitous and have pervasive impacts on cellular homeostasis. RNA is vulnerable to oxidative chemical alterations from myriad endogenous and exogenous sources. The most common chemical modification resulting from ROS exposure to RNA is 8-oxo-7,8-dihydroguanine (8-oxoG). While 8-oxoG modifications are known to impact mRNA processing, understanding the broader biological impact of 8-oxoG requires knowledge of how these modifications accumulate. In this work, we assessed the disparate enrichment of 8-oxoG modifications within RNAs in the E. coli transcriptome using an RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing technique with a high-affinity 8-oxoG antibody (8-oxoG-RIP-Seq). Our investigation of the RNA 8-oxoG enrichment landscape uncovered intrinsic RNA characteristics that correlate with 8-oxoG enrichment. These findings suggest intrinsic characteristics of RNA, most notably relative abundance, CDS length and G‑nucleotide composition, significantly influence RNA 8-oxoG accumulation. We harnessed these properties to construct a simple multiple linear regression model that predicts RNA 8-oxoG accumulation, which we validated in E. coli. This model was subsequently applied to predict 8-oxoG‑enriched RNA species in four other bacterial species spanning a wide range of oxidative stress tolerances; these predictions suggest that 8-oxoG accumulation is species dependent, with limited overlap in RNAs and functional pathways that are more susceptible to 8-oxoG accumulation. Further evaluation of this model in the extremophile D. radiodurans revealed a substantial reduction in predictive power. Overall, these findings better inform understanding of RNA 8-oxoG patterns in bacteria and have broader impacts towards advancing knowledge of the connection between RNA oxidation and cellular homeostasis.

title: PLD2 fuels 5‑fluorouracil resistance in colorectal cancer: Hypoxic hijacking of autophagy unveils a novel therapeutic vulnerability.
abstract: The present study investigated the relationship between phospholipase D2 (PLD2) and hypoxia‑induced chemoresistance in colorectal cancer (CRC) and elucidated its regulatory mechanisms. The present study demonstrated that increased PLD2 was associated with poor prognosis and chemoresistance in CRC via The University of Alabama at Birmingham cancer data analysis portal and Kaplan‑Meier plotter databases and 5‑fluorouracil (5‑Fu)‑resistant CRC tissues. The protein expression of PLD2, hypoxia‑inducible factor 1 alpha (HIF‑1α), multidrug resistance‑associated protein 2 (MRP2), LC3‑II/I, and Beclin‑1 was markedly upregulated under hypoxia in SW620 and SW480 cells in a time‑dependent manner. Next, SW620 and SW480 cells were transduced with recombinant replication‑deficient adenoviral vectors encoding PLD2‑targeting short hairpin (sh)RNA (Ad‑sh‑PLD2) or PLD2 overexpression (oe) constructs (Ad‑oe‑PLD2), followed by treatment with 5‑Fu, rapamycin (Rapa), or 3‑methyladenine (3‑MA), either alone or in combination.
